content.snl: %Two sets $A$ and $B$ are equal, denoted $A = B$, if and only if they have exactly the same elements. Formally, $A = B \iff (\forall x)(x \in A \iff x \in B)$. This axiom captures the principle that a set is completely determined by its elements.%
%Set theory is the mathematical study of sets, which are abstract collections of objects. It serves as a foundational framework for nearly all of modern mathematics.%
%Let $A$ be a set and $x$ an object. We write $x \in A$ if $x$ is an element of $A$, and $x \notin A$ otherwise. The symbol $\in$ is read as "is an element of" or "belongs to".%
%There exists a unique set containing no elements, called the empty set and denoted $\emptyset$. For any object $x$, we have $x \notin \emptyset$.%

%Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Their intersection, denoted $A \cap B$, is the set of all elements that belong to both $A$ and $B$. Formally, $A \cap B = \{\, x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \in B \,\}$. Two sets are called disjoint if $A \cap B = \emptyset$.%

%The power set of a set $A$, denoted $\mathcal{P}(A)$, is the set of all subsets of $A$. Formally, $\mathcal{P}(A) = \{\, B \mid B \subseteq A \,\}$. Note that $\emptyset \in \mathcal{P}(A)$ and $A \in \mathcal{P}(A)$ for any set $A$.%

%Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. We say $A$ is a proper subset of $B$, denoted $A \subsetneq B$, if $A \subseteq B$ and $A \neq B$. That is, every element of $A$ is in $B$, but there exists at least one element of $B$ that is not in $A$.%

%A set is a collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right. The objects in a set are called its elements or members. We typically denote sets by capital letters $A, B, C, \ldots$ and elements by lowercase letters $x, y, z, \ldots$.%

%Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. The set difference $A \setminus B$ is the set of all elements of $A$ that are not elements of $B$. Formally, $A \setminus B = \{\, x \in A \mid x \notin B \,\}$. Note that $A \setminus B$ is generally different from $B \setminus A$.%

%Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. We say $A$ is a subset of $B$, denoted $A \subseteq B$, if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$. Formally, $A \subseteq B$ means $(\forall x)(x \in A \implies x \in B)$. We also say $B$ is a superset of $A$, denoted $B \supseteq A$.%
%Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Their union, denoted $A \cup B$, is the set of all elements that belong to $A$, to $B$, or to both. Formally, $A \cup B = \{\, x \mid x \in A \text{ or } x \in B \,\}$.%
%We introduce the fundamental notions of set theory: sets, elements, equality, subsets, and the power set.%
%We define the basic operations on sets: union, intersection, and set difference.%
